summary: A white paper with personal opinions on IPng engineering considerations, drawing on experience with the DECnet Phase V transition. It suggests splitting IPng decisions and transition tasks into smaller parts. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This white paper gives personal recommendations for planning IPng. It proposes splitting the work into smaller decisions and letting service managers adapt transition plans to local conditions.

questions: how did rfc 1670 recommend planning ipng
subtitle: Personal recommendations for organizing IPng decisions and transition work.

tldr.problem: The memo argues that IPng decisions and transition work involve different technical and administrative tasks with different timelines.
tldr.mechanism: It recommends dividing work into areas such as addressing, name service, host software, and routing, then allowing experts and service managers to plan those areas in parallel.
tldr.outcome: It proposes local transition autonomy, tools and scenarios for service managers, and early decisions on address structure.

today: RFC 1670 is Informational and records one author's personal views on IPng engineering and transition planning. It does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Divide IPng Work into Smaller Parts
sections.content:
The author draws on experience with the DECnet Phase V transition and recommends dividing IPng decisions and transition tasks into smaller parts. The memo names address structure and allocation, name service, host software and programming interfaces, and routing protocols as separate areas.

Although these areas are related, the author argues that not every detail needs to be decided by the same date. Work can proceed in parallel while hard-to-change decisions receive early attention.
sections.plainLanguage: The author recommends treating IPng as several related projects rather than one large decision. Different experts can work on separate parts at the same time.

sections.title: Planning for Different Timelines
sections.content:
The memo says administrative changes, including those related to address changes, need the greatest implementation time, while routing-protocol changes need the least. It calls for an early decision on address structure so service managers can plan.

The author says some hosts may never be upgraded and may need to be phased out or operate with reduced connectivity. A lead time of 10 years or more is suggested to ease technical, financial, and organizational constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Some changes, especially administrative ones, need much more lead time than routing updates. The author proposes giving service managers early information and time to plan.

sections.title: Local Transition and Feedback
sections.content:
The memo says transition decisions require knowledge of local financial, political, and technical conditions. It recommends giving service managers tools, scenarios based on real examples, and information about the merits and limits of different strategies.

Systems and sites should be able to transition at different times. The author also recommends keeping an up-to-date list of software changes and using feedback from experience to improve software.
sections.plainLanguage: Each site should be able to move at a time that suits its conditions. Tools, examples, and feedback can help its service managers make informed choices.

sections.title: Configuration and Network Management
sections.content:
The author describes a need for tools that can send IP parameters, such as a system's address, default router, and local name servers, and collect information such as owner contact, location, and system name. The memo also calls for an easier way to update DNS and notes that automatic configuration could help when systems move between buildings.

It says address and routing hierarchies can support delegation of network management into subdomains.
sections.plainLanguage: Network managers need ways to configure systems, collect their details, and update DNS. The memo also connects address hierarchy with dividing management across subdomains.

references.text: Gross, P., ed., "Internet Next Generation Architecture", RFC 1550, December 1993.
